required_facts.statement: An iterable supplies an iterator via iter(value); an iterator supplies successive values via next(iterator) and signals exhaustion with StopIteration.
Separate iter(list_value) calls produce separate traversal state, while the list stores the reusable items.
Calling iter on an iterator returns that same iterator rather than a new independent traversal.
next(iterator, default) returns default when the iterator is exhausted instead of raising StopIteration.

teaching_blocks.content: A list stores reusable items, while an iterator records progress through a traversal. Keeping those roles separate explains why a fresh iterator and the same iterator behave differently.
An iterable supplies an iterator via iter(value); an iterator supplies successive values via next(iterator) and signals exhaustion with StopIteration.

Separate iter(list_value) calls produce separate traversal state, while the list stores the reusable items. Calling iter on an iterator returns that same iterator rather than a new independent traversal. next(iterator, default) returns default when the iterator is exhausted instead of raising StopIteration.

Advance one traversal without changing another:
```python
values = [3, 2]
first = iter(values)
second = iter(values)
print(next(first))
print(next(first))
print(next(first, None))
print(next(second))
print(iter(first) is first)
```
The results are 3, 2, None, 3 and True. Separate list iterators have separate traversal state. First is exhausted after two items, so next with a default returns None. Without the default, exhaustion signals StopIteration. Calling iter(first) returns that same iterator rather than resetting its progress.
An iterable source and its iterator are not interchangeable traversal states. Calling iter on an iterator does not create an independent restarted pass.

required_facts.statement: A function containing yield creates a generator iterator when called; advancing it runs until the next yield.
yield value supplies one item and suspends execution, retaining local state until the next advance.
Write a for loop and a condition inside a generator function, yielding each accepted item; reaching the function’s end terminates iteration.

teaching_blocks.content: A helper should supply accepted quantities one at a time. Yield gives a value and suspends the function rather than completing an ordinary return-style calculation.
A function containing yield creates a generator iterator when called; advancing it runs until the next yield.

yield value supplies one item and suspends execution, retaining local state until the next advance. Write a for loop and a condition inside a generator function, yielding each accepted item; reaching the function’s end terminates iteration.

Advance a generator function:
```python
def positive_quantities(values):
    for value in values:
        if value > 0:
            yield value

quantities = positive_quantities([3, -1, 2])
print(next(quantities))
print(next(quantities))
```
The outputs are 3 and 2. Calling the function creates a generator iterator. Advancing it runs to the next accepted yield, suspends there and retains local state for the next advance. The rejected minus one contributes no item. A later advance reaches the function's end and terminates iteration.
Yield does not finish the whole generator the way an ordinary return expression ends a call. It supplies an item while retaining state for a later advance.

(expression for item in iterable if condition) defines a generator that transforms accepted items lazily; the filtering if clause is optional.

The leftmost iterable expression is evaluated immediately, while item transformations and filtering happen during iteration. Pass a generator expression as the sole argument to sum to total transformed values without creating an intermediate list.

coverage.learning_objective: Account for iterator consumption and exhaustion.

required_facts.statement: Each next(iterator) consumes the next available item; a traversal or consumer sees only the remaining items.
Once an iterator raises StopIteration, it must continue to do so on subsequent calls.
iter(iterator) returns the same iterator and does not reset it.
For another pass over a reusable collection, obtain a fresh iterator from that collection rather than reusing its exhausted iterator.

teaching_blocks.content: A diagnostic has already consumed one item from a traversal. The following consumer sees only what remains, and iter on that iterator will not rewind it.
Each next(iterator) consumes the next available item; a traversal or consumer sees only the remaining items.

Once an iterator raises StopIteration, it must continue to do so on subsequent calls. iter(iterator) returns the same iterator and does not reset it. For another pass over a reusable collection, obtain a fresh iterator from that collection rather than reusing its exhausted iterator.

Observe consumption and a fresh pass:
```python
values = [3, 2]
traversal = iter(values)
print(next(traversal))
print(list(traversal))
print(list(iter(traversal)))
print(list(iter(values)))
```
The outputs are 3, [2], [], and [3, 2]. The exhausted traversal stays exhausted. Iter(traversal) returns that same iterator, whereas iter(values) supplies a fresh traversal of the reusable list. For a second complete pass, obtain that fresh iterator rather than reusing the consumed one.
Inspecting an iterator with next changes what later consumers can see. Calling iter on it does not reset it after inspection or exhaustion.

coverage.learning_objective: Choose eager or lazy processing for an iterable workload.

required_facts.statement: list(iterable) materializes its remaining items into a list that can be traversed repeatedly.
Generator expressions compute values as consumed and tend to use less memory than equivalent list comprehensions.
For a one-pass total, sum(expression for item in iterable) avoids constructing an intermediate transformed list.
An iterator is consumed as it advances and stays exhausted after completion, so repeated reuse may require a stored collection or a new source traversal.

teaching_blocks.content: A report may need one total or several passes over transformed values. Choose between lazy consumption and materialization based on which reuse the example requires.
list(iterable) materializes its remaining items into a list that can be traversed repeatedly.

Generator expressions compute values as consumed and tend to use less memory than equivalent list comprehensions. For a one-pass total, sum(expression for item in iterable) avoids constructing an intermediate transformed list. An iterator is consumed as it advances and stays exhausted after completion, so repeated reuse may require a stored collection or a new source traversal.

Compare a consumed generator with a stored result:
```python
values = [3, 2]
lazy = (value * 2 for value in values)
print(sum(lazy))
print(list(lazy))
stored = list(value * 2 for value in values)
print(sum(stored))
print(sum(stored))
```
The outputs are 10, [], 10 and 10. List materializes remaining items into a reusable collection. Generator expressions compute as consumed and tend to use less memory than equivalent list comprehensions. For a single total, sum(value * 2 for value in values) avoids the intermediate list.
Lazy does not mean automatically reusable. An iterator remains exhausted after completion; repeated work may need a stored collection or a new source traversal.

teaching_blocks.content: Two batches of quantities need one combined total. Chain traverses the first batch and then the second without first joining them into a list.
After from itertools import chain, chain(first, second) traverses each input in order, exhausting the first before moving to the second, without first concatenating them into a list.
sum(chain(first, second)) totals numeric items from the combined traversal.

Use the combined traversal directly:
```python
from itertools import chain
first = [3, 2]
second = [5, 4]
print(list(chain(first, second)))
print(sum(chain(first, second)))
```
The displayed sequence is [3, 2, 5, 4], and the total is 14. Each call here creates a combined traversal for its consumer. Chain exhausts the first input before moving to the second; it does not alternate items from the two batches. The total does not require constructing that displayed list first.
Chain is sequential concatenation of traversal, not pairwise zip. Interpret the inputs in order: first is exhausted before second is visited.

context.concept_name: Choosing map or filter for iterable transformations

coverage.learning_objective: Choose a readable iterable transformation idiom.

required_facts.statement: map(function, iterable) lazily applies a callable to successive items and yields the results.

Use a parenthesized generator expression instead of a list comprehension when preserving lazy traversal is required.

teaching_blocks.content: A transformation pipeline should select positive quantities and double them. Map, filter and comprehension forms can express this work with different materialization choices.
map(function, iterable) lazily applies a callable to successive items and yields the results.

filter(predicate, iterable) lazily yields items for which the predicate is true; filter(None, iterable) keeps truthy items. filter(predicate, iterable) corresponds to (item for item in iterable if predicate(item)). [function(item) for item in iterable if predicate(item)] makes a materialized transform-and-filter list and can replace a map/filter composition when that form communicates the computation more clearly. Use a parenthesized generator expression instead of a list comprehension when preserving lazy traversal is required.

Name the callable and predicate:
```python
def positive(value):
    return value > 0

def double(value):
    return value * 2

values = [3, -1, 2]
lazy = map(double, filter(positive, values))
print(list(lazy))
print([double(value) for value in values if positive(value)])
```
Both displayed lists are [6, 4]. Map and filter are lazy; the list call consumes the pipeline. The comprehension directly materializes its transform-and-filter result. Filter(positive, values) corresponds to (value for value in values if positive(value)); filter(None, values) instead selects truthy items.
Replacing a lazy pipeline with a list comprehension changes materialization. Use a parenthesized generator expression instead when preserving lazy traversal is required.

teaching_blocks.content: A test runner report is evidence only for the tests it actually executed. Read the count and distinguish unsuccessful assertions from unexpected exceptions.
python -m unittest test_module runs a named test module, and python -m unittest discover invokes test discovery.

Discovery defaults to the current directory and test*.py filenames; -s selects a starting directory and -p selects a filename pattern. A failure is an unsuccessful assertion check; the runner report identifies the test and traceback for the failed assertion. An error is an unexpected exception during a test rather than an explicitly failed assertion. The reported test count records how many tests ran; a count of zero supplies no executed checks of the helper’s behavior.

For an illustrative test_cost.py module, python -m unittest test_cost runs the named module. Python -m unittest discover uses discovery, with the current directory and test*.py names as defaults. The -s option selects another starting directory and -p selects a filename pattern. In the report, a failure identifies an unsuccessful assertion and its traceback; an error identifies an unexpected exception during a test. A reported count of zero means no helper checks ran, even if you intended to discover several.
A zero test count is not evidence of correct helper behavior. Also, failures and errors are different report categories, not two interchangeable descriptions of a failed assertion.

segments.summary: An unsuccessful equality assertion records a failure; raising an unexpected ValueError records an error. An assertion that correctly expects an exception can pass. Start diagnosis with the specific test case, exception type and result category, then use the traceback and test intent to understand the appropriate repair.

required_facts.statement: Define setUp(self) to initialize fresh per-test state before each test method; an error in setUp prevents that test method from running.
tearDown(self) runs after a test when setUp succeeded, including when the test failed.
self.addCleanup(function, *args, **kwargs) registers cleanup that runs after tearDown, or after a failed setUp; registered actions run in reverse registration order.
Register the release callable after acquiring the supplied test resource and store mutable test data on self in setUp rather than in shared class attributes.

teaching_blocks.content: Each test needs fresh mutable data, and a supplied resource needs cleanup even on setup failure. Arrange per-test state and registered release actions explicitly.
Define setUp(self) to initialize fresh per-test state before each test method; an error in setUp prevents that test method from running.

tearDown(self) runs after a test when setUp succeeded, including when the test failed. self.addCleanup(function, *args, **kwargs) registers cleanup that runs after tearDown, or after a failed setUp; registered actions run in reverse registration order. Register the release callable after acquiring the supplied test resource and store mutable test data on self in setUp rather than in shared class attributes.

For list state, define setUp(self) and assign self.quantities = [3, 2] there. Every test receives fresh per-test setup rather than mutating a shared class list. TearDown runs after a test whenever setUp succeeded, even if the test failed. For a supplied acquired resource, register its release callable with self.addCleanup(release) after acquisition. Registered cleanups run after tearDown, or after failed setUp, in reverse registration order. Trace acquisition and registration as separate steps when reasoning about a failing setup.
TearDown does not run when setUp fails. Registered cleanup covers that case; also, setUp failure prevents the test method from running.

video_need.reason: An execution-order diagram can contrast successful setup, failing tests, failed setup and reverse-order registered cleanup.

practice_anchor.objective: Implement TestCase.setUp to assign fresh self.quantities = [3, 2] and register the supplied release callable immediately after the supplied resource-acquisition step.
practice_anchor.success: Each test starts with quantities [3, 2], regardless of mutations in another test. The supplied resource is released after normal completion, test failure, and a setup failure occurring after cleanup registration.

live_code.required_skill: Initialize per-test instance state and register a callable with self.addCleanup without calling it immediately.
live_code.starter_state_intent: Provide a TestCase skeleton, supplied acquisition and release callables, and tests using only quantities as mutable test data. Leave setUp initialization and cleanup registration unfinished. Supply checks for normal completion, test failure, and failure after cleanup registration.
live_code.observable_success: The supplied checks confirm that every test begins with a distinct quantities list containing [3, 2], and that the release callable runs even when setup fails after registration.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show successful setup followed by a passing or failing test, tearDown, and reverse-registration-order cleanup. Contrast failed setup, which skips the test and tearDown but still runs already registered cleanups. Mark resource acquisition and cleanup registration as separate steps.

coverage.learning_objective: Explain generated code in terms of the stated requirements.

required_facts.statement: Trace each supplied input through the conditions to its actual return; a path reaching the end of a function without a return produces None.
Track each assignment and selected branch in order to determine the actual data and control flow for valid and invalid inputs.
Code from a virtual assistant can be mistaken, so check its behavior rather than treating its generated form as proof of correctness.

teaching_blocks.content: A generated helper looks plausible, but its actual branches must meet the supplied requirement. Trace specific inputs rather than treating generated form as proof.
Trace each supplied input through the conditions to its actual return; a path reaching the end of a function without a return produces None.

Track each assignment and selected branch in order to determine the actual data and control flow for valid and invalid inputs. Code from a virtual assistant can be mistaken, so check its behavior rather than treating its generated form as proof of correctness.

Consider this deliberately incomplete helper:
```python
def cost(quantity):
    if quantity > 0:
        return quantity * 4

print(cost(3))
print(cost(0))
```
The results are 12 and None. For three, the condition selects the return. For zero, the branch is not selected and the function reaches its end without return. If the supplied requirement expects zero cost for zero quantity, that traced None is a mismatch. Track each assignment, condition and actual return for valid and invalid inputs before deciding how the code should be corrected.
Plausible generated code is not correctness evidence. A missing return path produces None, not the value suggested by a comment or the user's intended calculation.

video_need.reason: Seeing the example execute, with the relevant values and control flow annotated, adds a changing-state demonstration to the text.

practice_anchor.objective: Annotate how the generated cost helper handles quantity 3 and an invalid quantity of -1, recording the selected branch and actual return for each.
practice_anchor.success: The annotations show that quantity 3 selects the positive branch and returns 12, while quantity -1 skips that branch and returns None implicitly. They identify the unmet requirement that invalid quantities must return 0.

live_code.required_skill: Trace supplied inputs through a generated function and compare actual returns with stated requirements.
live_code.starter_state_intent: Provide the unchanged cost(quantity) helper from the teaching example, with calls using 3 and -1. State that positive quantities must return quantity multiplied by 4 and invalid nonpositive quantities must return 0. Leave space for trace annotations using comments.
live_code.observable_success: Without changing the helper, the learner annotates each input binding, condition result, selected or skipped branch, and actual return. The learner distinguishes the explicit return of 12 from the implicit None and records the invalid-input requirement mismatch.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the two execution paths visible beside the cost helper: quantity 3 follows the explicit return, while quantity -1 skips the branch and reaches the function end, producing None rather than the required 0.

context.concept_name: Reviewing generated Python file operations for safety

coverage.learning_objective: Check generated Python code for destructive filesystem behavior.

required_facts.statement: Opening a file in w mode truncates existing content; inspect generated mode choices to identify an unintended overwrite.
Path.unlink() removes the file or symbolic link at that path; remove an unintended unlink call instead of executing it.
Path.rename(target) moves an entry and can replace an existing file on Unix; inspect the actual source and destination paths.

An absolute child path replaces a preceding base path, and a relative rename target is interpreted against the working directory; trace these path rules to check the actual destination before execution.

teaching_blocks.content: A generated report helper may overwrite or move a file somewhere unintended. Review the modes and resolved paths before allowing the operation to run.
Opening a file in w mode truncates existing content; inspect generated mode choices to identify an unintended overwrite.

Path.unlink() removes the file or symbolic link at that path; remove an unintended unlink call instead of executing it. Path.rename(target) moves an entry and can replace an existing file on Unix; inspect the actual source and destination paths. An absolute child path replaces a preceding base path, and a relative rename target is interpreted against the working directory; trace these path rules to check the actual destination before execution.

In a supplied helper, with open(output, "w") truncates an existing output. If that contradicts the requirement, do not execute it unchanged. A path.unlink() removes the file or symbolic link at that path; remove an unintended unlink call instead of trying it. For source.rename(target), inspect both source and destination, including the Unix possibility of replacing an existing file. Trace absolute child operands, which replace a preceding base, and relative rename targets, which resolve against the working directory. Write down the actual destination before execution.
A reassuring variable name such as safe_output does not establish a safe destination. Actual modes and path-resolution rules determine the operation being proposed.

video_need.reason: An annotated, non-executing review can diagram proposed source/destination paths and identify destructive operations before they run.

practice_anchor.objective: Review a generated cleanup helper without executing its filesystem operations, and remove an unintended deletion.
practice_anchor.success: The unintended path.unlink() call is removed, the intended helper behavior is preserved, and review notes identify the overwrite risk and actual rename destination.

live_code.required_skill: Trace generated file operations and edit out an unintended deletion before execution.
live_code.starter_state_intent: Supply an uncalled generated helper using output, path, source, and target. Its stated requirement permits writing a disposable output and moving source to the specified destination, but requires preserving path. Include an unintended path.unlink() call, an absolute child operand in constructing output, and a relative target. Provide the working directory and existing-file state as comments so the learner can trace effects without running the helper.
live_code.observable_success: Static inspection shows that path.unlink() has been removed and the helper remains syntactically valid. Learner comments identify that opening output in w mode truncates existing content, that the absolute child replaces the base path, that the relative rename target uses the working directory, and that renaming can replace an existing destination file on Unix. No filesystem-changing call is executed.

visual_anchor.purpose: Show the helper with annotations connecting each destructive operation to its affected path, including the discarded base for an absolute child and the working-directory destination for a relative rename target.

context.concept_name: Reviewing untrusted input and arbitrary Python execution

coverage.learning_objective: Reject unsafe execution of untrusted input in generated Python code.

required_facts.statement: eval evaluates a Python expression and can execute arbitrary code, so it must not be used to process untrusted text.
exec executes Python code supplied as text or a code object and is unsafe for untrusted instructions.
Invoking a shell makes quoting and metacharacters a security responsibility; inspect shell=True and untrusted command construction for injection risk.
Replace execution-based parsing with a parser matching the expected data, such as int or float for numeric text and json.loads for JSON, with explicit validation and handling of malformed input.
Non-executing parsing is not unlimited resource safety: impose input-size limits for untrusted JSON because malicious input can consume substantial CPU and memory.

teaching_blocks.content: A generated parser must not execute untrusted text. Review execution mechanisms and choose a parser matching the data the requirement actually expects.
eval evaluates a Python expression and can execute arbitrary code, so it must not be used to process untrusted text.

exec executes Python code supplied as text or a code object and is unsafe for untrusted instructions. Invoking a shell makes quoting and metacharacters a security responsibility; inspect shell=True and untrusted command construction for injection risk. Replace execution-based parsing with a parser matching the expected data, such as int or float for numeric text and json.loads for JSON, with explicit validation and handling of malformed input. Non-executing parsing is not unlimited resource safety: impose input-size limits for untrusted JSON because malicious input can consume substantial CPU and memory.

If the quantity arrives as untrusted text, replace a proposed eval(text) calculation with int(text) or float(text) as appropriate, followed by explicit value validation and malformed-input handling. For expected JSON, json.loads is the matching parser, but impose input-size limits because malicious input can consume substantial CPU and memory. Reject exec on untrusted instructions. Inspect shell=True and untrusted command construction for injection risk: a shell makes quoting and metacharacters a security responsibility. Review these calls as text; do not demonstrate them by running untrusted input.
Non-executing parsing does not imply unlimited resource safety. JSON needs input-size limits for untrusted input, and eval or exec must not be used to process untrusted text or instructions.

video_need.reason: Annotated code and data-flow diagrams can expose execution boundaries and unsafe input routes without executing hazardous examples.

practice_anchor.objective: Replace a generated eval-based quantity parser with int(text), handle malformed input, and validate that quantity is non-negative without executing untrusted text.
practice_anchor.success: Valid non-negative integer text produces the expected quantity. Malformed text and negative quantities produce quantity = None without an uncaught conversion error. The repaired parser contains no eval, exec, or shell invocation.

live_code.required_skill: Convert untrusted numeric text with int, handle ValueError, and validate the resulting quantity explicitly.
live_code.starter_state_intent: Provide text and quantity variables with a commented, non-executable eval(text) proposal for parsing quantity. State that quantity must be a non-negative integer and that rejected input must leave quantity as None.
live_code.observable_success: Inspect quantity after separate runs with valid integer text, malformed text, and negative integer text. Confirm the expected integer or None result and inspect the repaired source to verify that it never executes the supplied text.

visual_anchor.purpose: Make the boundary between untrusted text and execution visible in annotated, non-executable unsafe examples, alongside a repaired quantity parser showing int conversion, malformed-input handling, and explicit value validation.

context.concept_name: Accepting, repairing or rejecting generated Python on evidence

coverage.learning_objective: Decide whether generated Python code is acceptable using evidence.

required_facts.statement: Generated code can be wrong; test code obtained from a virtual assistant rather than accepting it solely because it was generated.
Use the supplied failed assertions and unexpected exceptions to identify behavior requiring correction; these results do not support accepting the helper unchanged.

Compare traced returns and supplied test expectations with the required behavior; record acceptance only for behavior supported by that evidence, and record correction when a mismatch can be addressed.
Reject execution of a proposed implementation that evaluates untrusted input or truncates a file contrary to the requirements until those unsafe operations are removed or corrected.

teaching_blocks.content: A generated implementation needs an evidence-based decision: accept supported behavior, correct a mismatch or refuse unsafe execution. Keep the requirement, traces and supplied tests together.
Generated code can be wrong; test code obtained from a virtual assistant rather than accepting it solely because it was generated.

Use the supplied failed assertions and unexpected exceptions to identify behavior requiring correction; these results do not support accepting the helper unchanged. Compare traced returns and supplied test expectations with the required behavior; record acceptance only for behavior supported by that evidence, and record correction when a mismatch can be addressed. Reject execution of a proposed implementation that evaluates untrusted input or truncates a file contrary to the requirements until those unsafe operations are removed or corrected.

Suppose the supplied expectation is cost(0) == 0, but the traced helper reaches its end and returns None. That mismatch supports correction, not unchanged acceptance. A failed assertion or unexpected test exception likewise identifies behavior needing correction. Record acceptance only for behavior supported by traced returns and supplied expectations. If the proposal evaluates untrusted input or truncates a file contrary to requirements, reject its execution until those operations are removed or corrected. Testing is necessary because assistant-generated code can be wrong.
Generated origin is not acceptance evidence. Neither failed tests nor identified unsafe operations support accepting the implementation unchanged.

video_need.reason: An annotated execution helps connect the interface to its result, although the written example supplies the essential explanation.

media.group_title: Decide from requirements and test evidence

segments.label: Repair a generated discount helper using expected results
segments.summary: A generated discount helper runs successfully and returns 80 for a price of 100 with a 20% discount. That result hides a mistake: the helper subtracts 20 as a fixed amount rather than calculating 20% of the price. With a price of 200, it returns 180 instead of the required 160. The repair calculates the discount amount as price multiplied by discount divided by 100, then subtracts that amount. Assertions for both expected results pass after the repair. Generated code and one passing test are not enough to establish correctness; acceptance needs evidence that the behavior matches the requirements.

bridge_note.before: Watch how one passing test hides a requirement mismatch, while a second input exposes it. Focus on the evidence supporting correction and verification, not the generated origin.
bridge_note.after: The clip demonstrates a requirement mismatch and verified repair, but not failed assertions, unexpected exceptions or unsafe-operation rejection. The text explains how those findings affect correction and rejection decisions.

practice_anchor.objective: Review supplied versions of the cost helper against their requirements, traced returns, safety findings and test results. Record an accept, correct or reject decision with an evidence-based justification for each version, without executing unsafe proposals.
practice_anchor.success: Recorded decisions accept only behavior supported by the supplied evidence, require correction for addressable mismatches or unexpected failures, and reject execution when untrusted input is evaluated or a file is truncated contrary to requirements.

live_code.required_skill: Read supplied Python and review evidence, then use Python assignments and string literals to record justified acceptance, correction or rejection decisions.

Keep proposed unsafe implementations non-executable; supply the testing evidence rather than requiring learners to construct tests.
live_code.observable_success: Python string assignments record a decision and cite the relevant requirement and supplied evidence for each cost version. No unsafe proposal is executed, and no failing or unsafe version is accepted unchanged.

visual_anchor.purpose: Place each cost helper's required behavior beside its traced return, supplied test result and safety finding, with the resulting accept, correct or reject decision and its justification visible.
